newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's speciality exporters shrug off strong lira.
newsitem.headline: Italy's speciality exporters shrug off strong lira.

text.p: Exporters of traditionally Italian goods from their homeland have seen little adverse effect from the recent strength of the lira this year, a report on trends in Italian exporters showed on Tuesday.

Indeed, exports of these typically Italian goods advanced in the first half of 1996 and showed little sign of flagging into the second half despite the lira's recent re-entry to Europe's currency grid, the reports authors point out.

Many Italian industrialists and exporters have been critical of the lira's re-entry into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) just over a week ago at the relatively high rate of 990 lire per German mark as it could penalise Italian exporters.

The study by Milan's Catholic University and agro-industry and chemical giant Montedison pointed out that this group of Italian goods, produced from largely small and medium-sized firms, were a valuable export earners to keep Italy's trade balance firmly in the black.

The report identified three product groups with a high capacity to export which it termed "Made in Italy". These were first, fashion items such as designer clothes and leather goods; second, household goods such as furniture, kitchen utensils, and domestic electrical goods and thirdly Mediterranean foods such as olive oil and pasta.

This "Made in Italy" category made a positive net contribution to Italy's trade balance of 125.8 trillion lire ($81.9 billion) in 1995, and was a major reason behind Italy's 44.4 trillion lire trade surplus.
One of the authors, Alberto Quadrio Curzio said, "The devaluation of the lira in 1994-95 was one important reason for the success of 'Made in Italy' but it was not the only one".
Curzio, the dean of the University's political science facility, added that for the small and medium-sized companies in this category innovation, quality and design all played a part.

He added that although the lira had rebounded in early 1996, exports from the "Made in Italy" sector had continued to rise, and in the first half of 1996 the positive contribution rose six trillion lire to 65 trillion lire from the first half of 1995.

Montedison's Marco Fortis said that there were no signs that the strong lira had had an effect on exports, but he did point out that for many of the products, such as ceramics and kitchen utensils, price was not often of prime importance to buyers.

Montedison claims to be Italy's most international company with two-thirds of its sales outside Italy, and is Italy's number one company in terms of sales in most western European countries and the United States. ($ = 1535 Italian Lire)
